rows.rule_summary: A successful activation needs at least 10 QSOs made from the park within a single UTC day.
Activities at the same park, in the same location, on the same UTC day count as one activation, with the QSOs combined toward the ten needed.
Logs from an attempt that fell short of ten QSOs should still be submitted, so the hunters worked still get their credit.
Hunters never submit logs. Hunter credit is awarded from the activator's uploaded log.
Any band and mode the operator's licence class permits may be used, WARC bands included. POTA is not a contest.
Contacts through land repeaters do not count. A repeater may be used to arrange a direct contact, but the logged QSO must not be through one.
Satellite contacts are permitted. Log the band of the activator's transmit frequency.
Relaying callsigns, signal reports or park references through a third station is not permitted and invalidates the contact. Both stations must copy each other directly.
Every contact needs direct action by both operators. Fully automated contacts are prohibited.
The program sets no power limit of its own. FCC limits for the operator's licence class and band still apply, as does using no more power than the contact needs.
Activators may spot themselves, and anyone may spot or respot an activator. Spots clear roughly 30 minutes after the last one, or when marked QRT.
The activator and all equipment must be inside the park boundary and on public property. The park must be one on POTA's designated list and open to the public.

A park counts as open where the public has legal access, or where a permit is obtainable. It is closed where the managing agency says access is prohibited. Partial seasonal closures may still leave lawful access to the rest.
Activators may not trespass on private land to reach a park, and may not operate from private property even where it adjoins or sits inside the park.
Operating from a vehicle or RV is fine, provided it is parked on public property inside the park boundary.
Where a trail or river is itself the POTA entity rather than part of a bounded park, the operator and equipment must be on public property within 30.5 metres (100 feet) of its edge.
Two-fers and larger are allowed, but the operator and equipment must sit inside the area where every activated park's boundary overlaps, and a separate log goes in for each park.
A contact between an activator and a hunter who is also at a designated park counts as park-to-park. Every other activator rule still applies to it.
POTA's own maps are a guide only. The managing agency's official boundary is what governs, so check the park's own website when it matters.
Logs go in as ADIF from the activator, with callsign, date, time, band and mode required, and UTC used throughout. There is no deadline, but hunters wait on the upload for their credit.
Activations from aircraft are permitted where the contacts are made from the airspace directly above the park.
Licence conditions and local and federal law override anything in the POTA rules, and participation is at the operator's own risk.
